quote: We've only been renting it for about a little over a year, but, we've owned the home for a long time.
stewart_read: This answer is genuinely ambiguous on the hard homeowner-verification gate: is the customer currently renting this specific home from someone else, or do they own it and are describing a landlord/tenant history elsewhere? The rep says 'Okay. Very nice.' and moves on without clarifying who is actually on title for THIS address.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have parsed this as 'they own the home, currently self-renting is irrelevant phrasing' and judged clarification unnecessary — but nothing in the transcript shows that judgment was made; the rep simply didn't follow up.
coaching_implication: This should have been clarified before proceeding — renters cannot buy solar (dq_rules.not_homeowner) and the statement as given doesn't resolve whether the customer owns 1909 McFadden St. Coach the rep to always ask 'so are you the owner of this specific home?' when residence-length answers are ambiguous.

quote: I don't think that the panels will be able to get enough sun, for them to be super fully fully beneficial to you.
stewart_read: The rep reaches a shading disqualification based solely on a Google Maps glance, without asking which side of the roof the trees shade, roof pitch, or square footage available on the unshaded side — verify items that would normally inform this call.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep could be following an internal heuristic that visible mature trees near a home are disqualifying regardless of orientation, making this a fast, policy-correct call rather than a shortcut. Nothing in the transcript supports this as trained policy though — the hedged phrasing ('I don't think') suggests it's the rep's own on-the-spot judgment, not a stated rule.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask 2-3 clarifying questions (which side of the roof, how many hours of direct sun, time of day the shade falls) before delivering a DQ based on a map image alone.

quote: But the trees really only only give shade on the portion of the house and only a part of the day, if that makes a difference.
stewart_read: The customer supplies a second, more granular counter-argument (partial shade, limited time of day) than their first, and the rep's next line ('It's a ton of space to put panels up there, unfortunately') does not engage with either specific detail raised.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have already mentally logged this as unresolvable without design-team input and was intentionally not litigating roof geometry on a cold call — a defensible scope-holding instinct. But the transcript shows no acknowledgment of the new detail at all, which reads as a miss rather than a deliberate deferral.
coaching_implication: Even when a rep can't personally resolve a technical question, acknowledging the specific detail ('got it — so it's really only shading the back part in the afternoon') keeps the customer feeling heard and gives the design team a sharper referral note than a generic escalation.

quote: So, yeah, I really do apologize, but I can get you off our list if you don't get any more calls. Okay?
stewart_read: The rep offers to remove the customer from the call list within seconds of a single map-based observation, before any pushback or further verification — this is a premature exit path being floated on a call that was otherwise going cooperatively.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as good-faith transparency (not wanting to waste the customer's time on repeated calls if genuinely disqualified) rather than a rush to end the call. However, the immediate customer pushback that follows suggests the DQ was delivered before the customer felt the case had actually been made.
coaching_implication: Slow down before offering list-removal; it signals finality to the customer and can shut down a conversation that a few more questions might have kept open.

quote: I can reach out to my design team and see if they would be able to do anything. And then if they can, I'll give you a callback, and we could totally get you scheduled. Okay?
stewart_read: This is the call's only 'next step' and it has no date, no time, and is conditional on an internal review the rep doesn't control. It is the softest possible close on a customer who was actively engaged seconds earlier.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the shading uncertainty, a genuinely conditional callback may be the procedurally correct move rather than a failure to close — the rep can't book an appointment for a home that may not be viable. The issue isn't that it's conditional; it's that even the conditional step has no timeframe attached.
coaching_implication: Even a conditional callback should get an anchor: 'I'll have an answer from the design team by [day] and will call you back then.' Coach the rep to never end a call with an open-ended 'I'll call you' with no timeframe.

quote: I just work with our design team, so I help get those estimates and stuff up together for the home.

alternative_hypothesis: The rep does reference a lead source at 00:06 ('I got a request that you were looking into solar for your home'), which is a lighter-weight legitimacy anchor than the full script template but does address the 'why are you calling' question minimally.
